name: Tongue scraper

lead: A tongue scraper is a thin curved strip of metal or plastic drawn across the tongue to remove the coating of bacteria, food debris and shed cells. People use it to cut bad breath, which matters for close-up social presence.

Most bad breath comes from sulfur compounds made by bacteria in the coating on the tongue's surface, so scraping it off lowers them for a while. A 2006 Cochrane review of two trials with 40 participants reported a statistically significant short-term drop in volatile sulfur compounds, and later reviews report small short-term effects relative to toothbrushing. The practice goes back to Ayurvedic tradition.

paras: Users scrape from back to front once or twice a day, usually in the morning after brushing, and rinse the scraper. Fresher breath lasts for a few hours.

Side effects are minor: gagging, soreness or occasional bleeding if scraped too hard. Dental guidance is that breath that stays bad despite cleaning warrants a dental or medical check for gum disease or other causes.

angle.text: Users scrape the tongue to remove coating and the bacteria behind bad breath, for fresher breath in close-up settings. Studies report a short-lived drop in breath compounds after scraping.

lead: A tongue scraper, also called a tongue cleaner, is a small hand tool, typically a curved strip or loop of metal or plastic, drawn along the top surface of the tongue to remove the coating of bacteria, food debris and shed cells that can build up there. Tongue brushes and brush-backed toothbrush heads serve a similar purpose. [1] Tongue cleaning is less commonly practised than tooth brushing, flossing or mouthwash use. [1]

It is used mainly to reduce oral malodour (bad breath) and to lessen the white or coloured tongue coating, which Wikipedia says can result from diet, reduced saliva flow, poor oral hygiene or tongue anatomy. [1] The practice has a long history, including in Ayurvedic tradition, where metal scrapers were used. [1]

A 2006 Cochrane review of tongue scraping for halitosis included two trials with 40 participants in total and reported a statistically significant short-term reduction in volatile sulfur compounds with scrapers, but the data could not be pooled and the evidence was described as limited. [2][3] Later reviews reported small short-term effects relative to toothbrushing, with little evidence on medium-term or chronic halitosis. [4][5] Wikipedia states that there are no clear scientific conclusions on its benefit for bad breath. [1]
infobox: Metal or plastic strip or loop, brush, rake, circular scraper [1]
Reducing tongue coating and breath odour [1][2]
Gagging, discomfort, irritation if too aggressive [1]

paras: The tongue's rough surface and papillae retain microorganisms and debris, which can form a visible coating. [1] Cleaning devices include flexible plastic or metal straps, bristled brushes and rakes, circular devices with handles, and ergonomic shapes designed to lift the coating. Wikipedia notes that effectiveness varies with shape, dimensions, contact surface and materials, and that scrapers are generally inexpensive and durable. [1]

A regular toothbrush can also be used on the tongue, but Wikipedia says toothbrushes are considered less effective for this because of their size and design, and that some brush heads carry a textured back for the purpose. [1] An in vitro study examined an ultrasound tongue scraper's effect on bacteria and biofilm. [6]

Wikipedia reports that Ayurveda recommends tongue cleaning as part of daily hygiene to remove accumulated debris, with scrapers historically made from copper, silver, gold, tin or brass, and that tongue hygiene has also been practised for centuries in Africa, Arabia, Europe, South America and East Asia, using materials from wood to ivory, whalebone and tortoiseshell. Western practice was less emphasised, being largely limited to the affluent between the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries, and a variety of commercial devices appeared in the twentieth century. [1]

Bacteria on the tongue produce malodorous compounds, including volatile sulfur compounds from the breakdown of debris on the posterior tongue, and Wikipedia reports estimates that the tongue accounts for most cases of bad breath, with the remainder arising from the stomach, tonsils, food stuck between teeth, gum disease or cavities. [1] A 2004 comparative trial likewise cited an estimate that about 85 percent of halitosis originates in the mouth, half of it from tongue residues, with hydrogen sulfide and mercaptans the main components. [7] Scraping is intended to remove the coating together with its bacteria and substrates, and Wikipedia notes the tongue can serve as a reservoir for dental and periodontal pathogens. [1]
Human evidence is dominated by small, short-term trials of breath odour and tongue coating.

The 2006 Cochrane review found two randomized trials with 40 participants; its commentary in General Dentistry described tongue scrapers as showing short-term efficacy in reducing volatile sulfur compounds. [2][3] A 2010 systematic review of tongue scrapers and brushes compared with brushing alone examined volatile sulfur compound concentration, organoleptic scores and tongue coating. [4] A 2015 systematic review of medium-term efficacy of mechanical and chemical agents included 12 trials of at least two weeks and found that most reported benefits came from products with an active ingredient in a dentifrice or mouthwash; the added value of tongue cleaning over a mouthwash was assessed in only one study, and the authors cited very limited evidence. [5]

A 2001 crossover study of 30 subjects compared a specially designed tongue cleaner, a tongue scraper and a toothbrush for reducing oral volatile sulfur compounds. [8] A 2004 crossover trial compared a toothbrush with a scraper using a handheld sulfide monitor. [7] A 2012 crossover trial of 21 subjects tested a zinc acetate and chlorhexidine mouth rinse with and without scraping, and a 2011 double-blind trial examined scraper and rinses on bad breath. [9][10] A 2004 trial examined scraping and oral mutans streptococci, and a 2013 randomized trial examined short-term effects on tongue-dorsum microbiota in intra-oral halitosis. [11][12]

Several recent trials use tongue scraping as the comparator for antimicrobial photodynamic therapy: a 2022 meta-analysis of eight studies with 345 patients found photodynamic therapy, alone or with scraping, produced greater reductions in halitosis measures than scraping alone, and further randomized trials in children and adults compared photodynamic therapy, oral hygiene, scrapers and probiotics. [13][14][15][16] In hospital settings, an intensive-care trial compared standard brushing with a comprehensive protocol that included tongue scraping. [17]

Wikipedia reports that tongue cleaning can cause discomfort, gagging and vomiting if misused, and irritation or ulcers if used aggressively; it also cites a single reported case of possible infective endocarditis after bacteremia from tongue cleaner use, and says people with high-risk cardiac conditions may be more vulnerable. [1]

In T Nation threads, tongue scrapers are mentioned as part of breath and oral-care routines. A poster on a low-carbohydrate diet reported bad breath persisting despite brushing three times daily, scraping and mouthwash. [18] Another thread tip suggests adding a stainless steel scraper to an oral care routine, on the reasoning that it removes unwanted bacteria. [19] In a 2008 thread about a dry, tacky mouth, a poster asks whether the original poster scrapes his tongue, and in another thread about a white tongue a poster recommends a scraper once a day plus probiotics. [20][21]

lore.intro: Tongue scrapers appear in fitness-forum threads as a cheap addition to oral care, particularly for breath problems associated with low-carbohydrate diets and for a white tongue. [18][19][21]
